subject: science
question: What makes a meal balanced? Answer in about three sentences.
modelAnswer: A balanced meal contains all the nutrients the body needs — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. They must be there in the right amounts, not too much or too little of any one. It should also include roughage and enough water.

keyPoints.label: It has all the nutrients the body needs
In the right amounts — not too much of any one
It also includes roughage and water

subject: science
question: Ravi eats only rice for lunch every single day. Say what is wrong with that, and name two things he should eat as well.
modelAnswer: Rice is mostly carbohydrate, so it gives energy but very little else. He is missing protein, so he should take dal, egg or paneer. He is also missing vitamins and minerals, so he should take vegetables or fruit.

keyPoints.label: Rice supplies mainly carbohydrate — energy and little else
Missing protein — dal, pulses, egg, paneer, fish or meat
Missing vitamins and minerals — vegetables, fruit or salad

subject: science
question: Why does a farm labourer need more carbohydrate in a day than someone who sits in an office? Name one food that would give it.
modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are the body’s main source of energy. Heavy physical labour burns far more energy than sitting does, so a labourer needs a larger amount. Rice, wheat, potato and bread are foods that supply it.

keyPoints.label: Carbohydrates are the body’s main source of energy
Harder physical work burns more, so more is needed
A food that supplies it — rice, wheat, potato, bread

subject: science
question: Fats are often called bad, yet the body needs them. Explain why they are needed, and what happens if someone takes far too much.
modelAnswer: Fats store energy, and they give more energy than the same weight of carbohydrate. They also keep the body warm and protect the organs. Taking far too much leads to obesity and heart problems.

keyPoints.label: They store energy, and give more per gram than carbohydrate
They keep the body warm and cushion the organs
Too much causes obesity and heart trouble

subject: science
question: Amma throws away the water after boiling potatoes. Explain what is lost by doing that and what she could do instead.
modelAnswer: Vitamins and minerals dissolve into the boiling water, so throwing it away throws the nutrients away too. Vitamin C is destroyed especially easily. She could steam them instead, or keep the water and use it in soup or dough.

keyPoints.label: Nutrients dissolve into the water and are thrown out with it
Vitamins, especially vitamin C, are lost
Steam instead, or reuse the water in soup or dough

subject: science
question: Give two good reasons for cooking food before eating it.
modelAnswer: Cooking kills germs and harmful bacteria, so the food is safer. It makes food softer and easier to digest. It also improves the taste and smell, so people eat it more willingly.

keyPoints.label: It kills germs and makes food safe
It softens food and makes it easier to digest
It improves taste and smell

subject: science
question: A child bruises easily and their gums bleed when they brush. What is likely missing from their meals, what is the illness called, and what should they eat?
modelAnswer: They are probably short of vitamin C. The illness is called scurvy. Eating oranges, lemons, amla or guava would supply what is missing.

keyPoints.label: Vitamin C is missing
The disease is scurvy
Citrus fruit, amla or guava would supply it

subject: science
question: Explain what malnutrition means, and why a person can be malnourished even when they never feel hungry.
modelAnswer: Malnutrition means the body is not getting the nutrients it needs in the right amounts. Someone may eat plenty of food and still be short of protein, vitamins or minerals, because their meals lack variety. Their growth suffers and they fall ill easily.

keyPoints.label: The body is not getting the nutrients it needs
Plenty of food can still be short of some nutrient
Growth suffers and illness comes easily

subject: science
question: Trace how wheat reaches your kitchen from the field. Mention three stages.
modelAnswer: The farmer grows the crop and harvests it when it is ripe. The grain is then threshed and taken to a mill, where it is ground into flour. Traders and shops carry it to the market, where a family buys it.

keyPoints.label: The farmer grows and harvests the crop
It is threshed and milled into flour
It is transported and sold in shops or markets

subject: science
question: Why is it better for a family to buy vegetables grown nearby rather than ones brought from far away?
modelAnswer: Vegetables grown close by reach the shop soon after picking, so they are fresher and keep more of their vitamins. They cost less because there is little transport to pay for. It also supports the farmers of that area.

keyPoints.label: They are fresher, so they keep more of their nutrients
They cost less, with little transport to pay for
It supports farmers of that area

subject: science
question: Your friend has chips and a cold drink for lunch every day at school. Explain three things that are wrong with that.
modelAnswer: Those items are high in fat, salt and sugar, which causes weight gain and tooth decay. They have almost no protein, vitamins or minerals, so the body gets nothing to grow with. They also have no roughage, so digestion suffers.

keyPoints.label: High in fat, salt and sugar
Almost no protein, vitamins or minerals
Weight gain, tooth decay or poor digestion follow

subject: science
question: Millets are being encouraged again in India. Give three reasons why they are a good crop to grow and to eat.
modelAnswer: They are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, so they are very nourishing. They need little water and grow in dry land where rice would fail. They also store well and are cheap for a poor family to buy.

keyPoints.label: Rich in fibre, iron and calcium
They need little water and grow on dry land
They store well and are cheap

subject: science
question: A girl is pale, tired all the time and breathless after climbing stairs. Which mineral is she short of, what is the illness called, and what should she eat?
modelAnswer: She is short of iron. The illness is anaemia. Green leafy vegetables such as spinach, along with jaggery, dates and liver, would supply the iron she needs.

keyPoints.label: Iron is the mineral she lacks
The illness is anaemia
Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates or liver

subject: science
question: Explain why growing children are told to drink milk, and name two other foods that do the same job.
modelAnswer: Milk is rich in calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth. Without enough of it, bones stay weak and break easily. Curd, cheese, ragi and green leafy vegetables supply calcium too.

keyPoints.label: Milk supplies calcium
Calcium builds strong bones and teeth
Curd, cheese, ragi or leafy vegetables do the same

subject: science
question: Nutrients are grouped by the job they do in the body. Describe three of those jobs and give a food for each.
modelAnswer: Carbohydrates and fats are energy-giving, and rice or oil supplies them. Proteins are body-building and repair worn parts, and dal or egg supplies them. Vitamins and minerals are protective, keeping disease away, and fruit and vegetables supply them.

keyPoints.label: Energy-giving — carbohydrates and fats
Body-building and repair — proteins
Protective — vitamins and minerals keep disease away

subject: science
question: Two boys of the same age eat the same meals, but one plays football all evening and the other reads at home. Explain why their needs are not the same.
modelAnswer: Playing football uses up a great deal of energy, so the boy who plays needs more carbohydrate and fat to replace it. He also needs more protein, because active muscles have to be repaired and built. The boy who reads uses less, so eating the same amount would store as extra weight.

keyPoints.label: Physical activity uses up much more energy
So more carbohydrate, fat or protein is needed
Eating the same when less active stores as extra weight

subject: science
question: Why are proteins especially important for a growing child and someone recovering from an injury? Name two foods that supply them.
modelAnswer: Proteins build new cells and tissues, which is how a child grows taller. They also repair parts of the body that have been damaged, so a wound heals. Dal, egg, milk, paneer and fish supply them.

keyPoints.label: They build new cells and tissue, so the body grows
They repair damaged parts, so wounds heal
Dal, egg, milk, paneer or fish supply them

subject: science
question: A family does not eat meat, fish or eggs. Explain how they can still get what their bodies need to grow, and name two foods they could use.
modelAnswer: Plants supply protein as well as animals do, so nothing is missing in a vegetarian diet. Pulses such as dal and rajma, along with soya, groundnut, milk and paneer, are rich in it. Eating pulses together with cereals makes the protein work better still.

keyPoints.label: Plant foods supply protein just as animal foods do
Pulses, soya, groundnut, milk or paneer
Pulses with cereals together work better

subject: science
question: Roughage gives the body no energy at all, yet meals must contain it. Explain why, and name two foods that provide it.
modelAnswer: Roughage is the fibre from plants that the body cannot digest. It adds bulk and helps waste move through the intestine, so it prevents constipation. Whole grains, fruit, vegetables and salad provide it.

keyPoints.label: It is plant fibre the body cannot digest
It moves waste along and prevents constipation
Whole grains, fruit, vegetables and salad provide it

subject: science
question: Give three reasons the body needs plenty of water every day.
modelAnswer: Water carries digested food and oxygen around the body in the blood. It removes waste as urine and sweat. It also controls body temperature, because sweating cools a person down.

keyPoints.label: It carries food and oxygen around in the blood
It removes waste as urine and sweat
It controls temperature — sweating cools the body

subject: science
question: A boy cannot see properly once it gets dark, though his sight is fine in daylight. Say what he lacks, what the condition is called, and what would help.
modelAnswer: He lacks vitamin A. The condition is night blindness. Carrot, papaya, mango, milk and green leafy vegetables would supply the vitamin A he needs.

keyPoints.label: Vitamin A is missing
The condition is night blindness
Carrot, papaya, mango, milk or leafy vegetables

subject: science
question: Children are told to play outside in the morning sun. Explain what the body makes then, why it matters, and what happens without it.
modelAnswer: Sunlight lets the skin make vitamin D. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, which is needed for strong bones and teeth. Without it, bones become soft and bend, a disease called rickets.

keyPoints.label: The skin makes vitamin D from sunlight
It helps absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth
Without it bones soften and bend — rickets

subject: science
question: Describe how a butterfly changes from the time it hatches until it can fly. Name the stages in order.
modelAnswer: A caterpillar hatches from the egg and eats leaves constantly, growing fast. It then becomes a pupa inside a chrysalis, where it stays still and changes completely. Finally the adult emerges with wings.

keyPoints.label: A caterpillar or larva hatches and feeds
It becomes a pupa inside a chrysalis or cocoon
The adult emerges with wings

subject: science
question: A tadpole and a grown frog look nothing alike. Describe three ways the young one changes as it grows up.
modelAnswer: The tadpole breathes through gills in water, and later develops lungs so it can breathe air. It loses its tail as it grows. It also grows legs, the hind legs appearing before the front ones, so it can move on land.

keyPoints.label: Gills give way to lungs, so it can breathe air
The tail is lost
Legs grow — hind legs first, then the front ones

subject: science
question: A car moves, uses fuel and gives out gas, yet nobody calls it alive. Give three things a living creature does that a car cannot.
modelAnswer: A living creature grows by itself from young to adult, whereas a car is built at its full size. It reproduces, making young of its own kind. It also responds to what is around it and repairs itself when hurt.

keyPoints.label: It grows by itself
It reproduces — young of its own kind
It responds to surroundings and heals itself

subject: science
question: Plants stay rooted in one place all their lives. Explain how they still show movement and response, with an example.
modelAnswer: Plants move by growing rather than by walking. A shoot bends towards light, and roots grow downwards towards water. The touch-me-not folds its leaves the moment it is touched, which shows it responds too.

keyPoints.label: They move by growing, not by walking
Shoots turn to light, roots grow to water
The touch-me-not folds when touched

subject: science
question: Trace the life of a mango tree from the very beginning to the point where it can start the cycle again.
modelAnswer: It begins as a seed, which germinates when it gets water, warmth and air. A seedling grows into a sapling and then into a mature tree with roots, stem and leaves. The tree flowers, and the flowers become fruit carrying seeds, so the cycle starts again.

keyPoints.label: The seed germinates given water, warmth and air
It grows into a mature plant with roots, stem and leaves
It flowers, and flowers become fruit carrying new seeds

subject: science
question: Explain why a plant that never flowers can be a serious problem for a farmer.
modelAnswer: Flowers are the reproductive part, and without them no fruit can form. Without fruit there are no seeds, so nothing can be sown the following year. Many crops are grown precisely for their fruit or grain, so the farmer has nothing to harvest or sell.

keyPoints.label: Flowers are the reproductive part of the plant
No fruit means no seed for the next sowing
Nothing to harvest or sell

subject: science
question: Seeds kept dry in a tin for months do not sprout, but the same seeds sprout in a few days on wet cotton. Explain what the seed needs and why.
modelAnswer: A seed needs water, which softens the coat and wakes the sleeping embryo. It needs air, because the embryo has to respire to release energy. It also needs a suitable warmth, since it will not sprout when it is too cold.

keyPoints.label: Water softens the coat and wakes the embryo
Air, because the embryo must respire
Suitable warmth — it will not sprout when too cold

subject: science
question: Seeds have to travel away from the parent plant. Describe three ways they are carried, with an example of each.
modelAnswer: Wind carries light seeds with hairs or wings, like the drumstick and the dandelion. Water floats seeds such as the coconut to a new shore. Animals carry them, either by sticking to fur like the xanthium or by being eaten and dropped in their droppings.

keyPoints.label: Wind carries light, winged or hairy seeds
Water floats seeds such as the coconut
Animals carry them — stuck to fur, or eaten and dropped

subject: science
question: A box holds pins, rubber bands, paper clips and plastic buttons all jumbled together. Describe how you would quickly separate them, and why it works.
modelAnswer: Move a magnet through the mixture. The pins and clips are made of iron, which is attracted, so they cling to the magnet and lift out. Rubber and plastic are not attracted at all, so they stay behind in the box.

keyPoints.label: Pass a magnet through the mixture
Iron things — pins and clips — are attracted and lift out
Rubber and plastic are not attracted and stay behind

subject: science
question: Name two materials that a magnet pulls and two that it does not, and say what the first group have in common.
modelAnswer: Iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are pulled by a magnet. Wood, plastic, glass, rubber and paper are not. The first group are all metals of a particular kind, and materials that behave that way are called magnetic.

keyPoints.label: Iron, nickel, cobalt or steel are pulled
Wood, plastic, glass, rubber or paper are not
The first group are metals, called magnetic materials

subject: science
question: A bar magnet is rolled in iron filings and lifted out. Describe what you would see, and explain it.
modelAnswer: The filings cling in thick bunches at the two ends and hardly at all in the middle. That is because the pulling power is strongest at the ends, which are the poles. In the centre the force is weakest, so almost nothing sticks there.

keyPoints.label: Filings gather thickly at the two ends
The ends are the poles, where the force is strongest
The middle is weakest, so little sticks there

subject: science
question: A bar magnet is snapped cleanly in half. Say what each piece now has, and what that tells you about poles.
modelAnswer: Each half is a complete magnet with a north pole and a south pole of its own. You cannot obtain a single separated pole, however many times you break it. Poles always exist in pairs.

keyPoints.label: Each piece becomes a complete magnet
Each has its own north and south pole
A single pole can never be obtained — poles come in pairs

subject: science
question: State the rule about how two magnets behave when brought close, and give an example of each case.
modelAnswer: Unlike poles attract, so a north brought near a south pulls together. Like poles repel, so two norths push each other away. The rule is that like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

keyPoints.label: Unlike poles attract — north with south
Like poles repel — north with north
The pulling together is called attraction

subject: science
question: You are given two identical iron bars, one magnetised and one not, and told not to use anything else. Explain how you can tell which is which.
modelAnswer: Bring an end of the first bar near an end of the second and note what happens, then turn one bar around and try again. If they push apart in one of the positions, both are magnets. Plain iron is only ever attracted and never pushed away, so repulsion is the sure test.

keyPoints.label: Bring the ends near, then reverse one and try again
Pushing away proves it — repulsion is the sure test
Attraction alone proves nothing, since plain iron is attracted too

subject: science
question: Explain the difference between a natural and an artificial magnet, and give one example of each.
modelAnswer: A natural one is found in the ground as a rock — lodestone, which is an ore of iron. An artificial one is made by people from iron or steel. Bar magnets, horseshoe magnets and the magnets in a fridge door are all made ones.

keyPoints.label: Natural ones are found in the earth — lodestone
Artificial ones are made by people from iron or steel
Bar, horseshoe, needle or fridge magnets are made ones

subject: science
question: Why is a horseshoe shape used for a magnet meant to lift heavy loads, rather than a straight bar?
modelAnswer: Bending it brings both poles round to the same side, close together. The two pulls then act on the load at once instead of from opposite ends. That makes the lifting force much stronger than a straight one of the same size.

keyPoints.label: Bending brings both poles to the same side, close together
Both pulls act on the load at once
So the lifting force is much stronger

subject: science
question: Describe how you would turn an ordinary iron nail into a magnet using a bar magnet, and say how you would check that it worked.
modelAnswer: Stroke the nail with one pole of the bar magnet, always in the same direction, lifting it away and returning to the start each time. Repeat this thirty or forty times. Then hold the nail near some pins — if it picks them up, it has become a magnet.

keyPoints.label: Stroke it with one pole of the magnet
Always in the same direction, many times
Test it by picking up pins

subject: science
question: Give three things that would make a magnet lose its power, and one way to store magnets so it does not happen.
modelAnswer: Heating it strongly destroys the magnetism. Hammering or dropping it repeatedly does the same. Storing magnets carelessly weakens them too. They should be kept in pairs with unlike poles facing and a soft iron keeper across the ends.

keyPoints.label: Strong heating destroys it
Hammering or dropping does the same
Store in pairs with unlike poles facing, and a keeper

subject: science
question: A magnet is hung by a thread so it can turn freely, and left alone. Say what it does, and explain how sailors once used this.
modelAnswer: It swings round and comes to rest pointing north and south every time. That happens because the earth itself behaves like a huge magnet and pulls it round. Sailors used a magnetised needle floating on water as a compass, so they could steer with no land in sight.

keyPoints.label: It settles pointing north and south
Because the earth acts like a giant magnet
A compass let sailors steer out of sight of land

subject: science
question: You are lost in a forest with a needle, a piece of cork and a bowl of water, and the needle has been stroked with a magnet. Explain how these help.
modelAnswer: Lay the needle on the cork and float it on the water so it can turn freely without rubbing. It swings until it lines up pointing north and south. Once north is known, the other directions follow and you can walk a straight course.

keyPoints.label: Float the needle on the cork so it turns freely
It settles pointing north and south
Knowing north gives the other directions

subject: science
question: Describe three places a magnet is at work in ordinary life, and what job it does in each.
modelAnswer: A refrigerator door has one in its seal, so the door stays shut. A compass uses one to point out direction for a traveller. Huge ones on cranes lift scrap iron in a junkyard, and doctors use small ones to draw iron splinters out of a patient’s eye.

keyPoints.label: A fridge door, pencil box or cupboard catch
A compass, to find direction
Cranes lifting scrap, or removing iron splinters

subject: science
question: A rubbish heap has iron tins mixed with plastic and glass. Explain how a factory sorts them and why the method is better than doing it by hand.
modelAnswer: A large electromagnet is passed over the heap, and the iron tins are attracted and lift away while plastic and glass stay put. It is far faster than picking through by hand and handles a huge quantity. It is also safer, because nobody has to touch sharp or dirty rubbish.

keyPoints.label: A big electromagnet lifts the iron away
Plastic and glass are not attracted and stay behind
Much faster than by hand, and safer

subject: science
question: Tell the story of how magnets are said to have been discovered, and what the rock was called.
modelAnswer: A shepherd named Magnes was walking on a hillside when the iron nails of his sandals and the tip of his stick stuck fast to a rock. The rock was lodestone, an ore of iron that is naturally magnetic. The word magnet is said to come from his name, or from the place Magnesia.

keyPoints.label: A shepherd, Magnes, found his iron sticking to a rock
The rock was lodestone, a natural ore of iron
The name comes from Magnes or from Magnesia

subject: science
question: Explain why the compass mattered so much to people long ago, and what they had to rely on before it existed.
modelAnswer: Before it, travellers steered by the sun in the day and the pole star at night, which failed whenever the sky was cloudy. A compass works in any weather and at any hour, so ships could sail out of sight of land. That let traders and explorers cross open seas and reach places they had never seen.

keyPoints.label: They relied on the sun and stars, which clouds hid
A compass works in any weather, day or night
So ships could cross open sea, and trade and exploring grew

subject: science
question: Describe how a solid, a liquid and a gas differ in the way they hold their shape and fill a container.
modelAnswer: A solid keeps a fixed shape and a fixed volume, so a stone stays the same in any box. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of whatever holds it, as water does in a glass. A gas has neither, spreading out to fill the whole container.

keyPoints.label: A solid keeps a definite shape and volume
A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of the vessel
A gas spreads out and fills the whole space

subject: science
question: Explain what happens to ice as it is heated all the way to steam, naming the changes.
modelAnswer: Heating ice makes it melt into water, and that change is called melting. Heating the water further turns it into steam, which is boiling or evaporation. Cooling steam turns it back into water by condensation, so the changes can be reversed.

keyPoints.label: Solid to liquid — melting
Liquid to gas — boiling or evaporation
Cooling reverses it — condensation

subject: science
question: A steel pan is given a plastic handle. Explain the reason, using what you know about how heat travels.
modelAnswer: Steel is a good conductor, so heat passes quickly through it from the flame. Plastic is a poor conductor, an insulator, so heat hardly travels along it. The handle therefore stays cool enough to hold and the cook is not burnt.

keyPoints.label: Steel conducts heat well, so heat passes through quickly
Plastic is a poor conductor — an insulator
So the handle stays cool and nobody is burnt

subject: science
question: Electric wires are made of copper but wrapped in plastic. Explain why each of those two materials is chosen.
modelAnswer: Copper is a good conductor of electricity, so current flows through it easily. Plastic does not let current pass, so it is an insulator. The covering keeps the current inside the wire and stops anyone touching it from getting a shock.

keyPoints.label: Copper conducts electricity, so current flows easily
Plastic does not let current pass — an insulator
So nobody touching the wire gets a shock

subject: science
question: A huge ship made of iron floats, while a small iron nail sinks. Explain how that can be.
modelAnswer: Floating depends on density, not on weight alone. A ship is hollow and full of air, so the whole thing is less dense than water and it floats. A nail is solid iron, denser than water, so it goes straight down.

keyPoints.label: It depends on density, not weight alone
The ship is hollow and full of air, so overall it is lighter than water
The nail is solid, denser than water, so it sinks

subject: science
question: Explain what makes one material harder than another, and why a diamond is used to cut glass rather than the other way round.
modelAnswer: Hardness is how well something resists being scratched or cut. A harder material can scratch a softer one, but not the reverse. Diamond is the hardest natural substance, so it scratches glass easily while glass cannot mark it.

keyPoints.label: Hardness is resistance to being scratched or dented
A harder material scratches a softer one, never the reverse
Diamond is the hardest natural substance

subject: science
question: Sugar stirred into water seems to disappear, but sand does not. Explain what is happening in each case, using the right words.
modelAnswer: Sugar is soluble, so it dissolves and spreads evenly through the water to form a solution. It has not vanished — it is still there, and boiling the water away would leave it behind. Sand is insoluble, so it stays as separate grains and settles at the bottom.

keyPoints.label: Sugar is soluble and dissolves to form a solution
It has not vanished — it can be recovered
Sand is insoluble and settles at the bottom

subject: science
question: Sugar dissolves much faster in hot tea than in cold water. Give two reasons, and say what else would speed it up.
modelAnswer: Heat makes the particles move faster, so they mix more quickly. Hot liquid can also hold more dissolved sugar than cold. Stirring speeds it up as well, and so does grinding the sugar into smaller grains.

keyPoints.label: Heat makes particles move faster, so mixing is quicker
A hot liquid dissolves a greater amount
Stirring, or smaller grains, speeds it up

subject: science
question: Explain the difference between a pure substance and a mixture, giving an example of each.
modelAnswer: A pure substance has only one kind of material in it, such as distilled water or common salt. A mixture has two or more materials jumbled together, such as air, milk or sand in water. The parts of a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated again.

keyPoints.label: A pure substance contains only one kind of material
A mixture has two or more jumbled together
The parts keep their own properties and can be separated

subject: science
question: Give three reasons why people bother to separate the parts of a mixture at all.
modelAnswer: Sometimes the useful part must be taken out, as when butter is separated from milk. Sometimes a harmful or useless part must be removed, such as stones from rice. Sometimes it is to obtain something pure, as when salt is got from sea water.

keyPoints.label: To obtain the useful part
To remove a harmful or useless part
To obtain something pure

subject: science
question: Describe how a farmer separates grain from the light husk after harvest, and what the method depends on.
modelAnswer: The farmer drops the mixture from a height on a windy day, which is called winnowing. The wind blows the light husk to one side while the heavier grain falls straight down in a heap. It works because the two parts differ in weight.

keyPoints.label: The method is winnowing — dropping it in the wind
The light husk is blown aside, the heavy grain falls straight
It depends on the difference in weight

subject: science
question: Flour has to be separated from bran, and stones have to be taken out of rice. Describe the method used for each and why they differ.
modelAnswer: Flour is separated from bran by sieving, because the two differ in the size of their particles and the fine flour passes through the mesh. Stones are taken from rice by handpicking, since the pieces are few, large and easy to see. The method chosen always depends on how the parts differ.

keyPoints.label: Sieving separates by particle size
Handpicking, because the pieces are few and easy to see
The method depends on how the parts differ

subject: science
question: Muddy river water has to be made clear. Describe the steps, naming each one.
modelAnswer: The water is left standing so the heavier mud settles at the bottom, which is called sedimentation. The clear liquid above is then poured off gently without disturbing the settled layer, and that is decantation. Finally it is passed through a filter such as cloth or filter paper to trap the fine particles left behind.

keyPoints.label: Standing lets the heavier mud settle — sedimentation
Pouring off the clear liquid — decantation
Passing it through a filter traps the fine particles

subject: science
question: Explain why tea is poured through a strainer, and what would be left in it.
modelAnswer: The strainer acts as a filter with very small holes. The liquid tea passes through, while the solid leaves are too large and are held back. The used leaves stay in the strainer as the residue, and the liquid collected is the filtrate.

keyPoints.label: It works as a filter with very small holes
The liquid passes through, the solids are held back
Leaves left are the residue; the liquid is the filtrate

subject: science
question: Describe how salt is obtained from sea water on the coast, and why filtering would not work.
modelAnswer: Sea water is let into shallow pans and left in the sun and wind. The water evaporates into the air, leaving the salt behind as crystals to be gathered. Filtering fails because the salt is dissolved, so it passes straight through the paper with the water.

keyPoints.label: It is spread in shallow pans in sun and wind
The water evaporates and the salt is left as crystals
Filtering fails because dissolved salt passes through

subject: science
question: Explain how you would obtain drinkable water from salty water and still keep the water itself, not just the salt.
modelAnswer: The salty water is heated until it boils and turns to steam, leaving the salt behind in the vessel. The steam is led away and cooled, so it condenses back into liquid water. That collected water is pure, and the whole process is called distillation.

keyPoints.label: Heat it until it boils to steam, leaving the salt behind
Cool the steam so it condenses back to liquid
The process is distillation, and the water is pure

subject: science
question: When sugar is stirred into water, name the two parts by their proper terms and explain what each one is.
modelAnswer: The sugar is the solute, the substance that dissolves. The water is the solvent, the liquid that does the dissolving. Together they make a solution, and it is the same all the way through.

keyPoints.label: The sugar is the solute — the substance that dissolves
The water is the solvent — the liquid that dissolves it
Together they form a solution, uniform throughout

subject: science
question: A glass of water will take four spoons of sugar but not ten — the rest lies at the bottom. Explain what has happened and what would let it take more.
modelAnswer: The water has taken all it can hold at that temperature, so it is saturated. Any further sugar cannot dissolve and settles at the bottom instead. Heating the water lets it hold more, so the extra would then dissolve.

keyPoints.label: The water is saturated — it has taken all it can hold
The extra cannot dissolve and settles undissolved
Heating lets it hold more

subject: social-science
question: Explain the difference between a prejudice and a stereotype, giving an example of each from school life.
modelAnswer: A prejudice is judging someone before you know anything about them, such as deciding a new classmate is unfriendly because of where they come from. A stereotype fixes a whole group into one image, such as saying all boys are noisy. Both are unfair because they ignore what a person is actually like.

keyPoints.label: A prejudice is judging in advance, without knowing the person
A stereotype fixes a whole group into one fixed image
Both are unfair — they ignore what the person is really like

subject: social-science
question: A teacher always picks the same few pupils to answer questions and never the quiet ones. Explain what harm this can do over time.
modelAnswer: The pupils never chosen begin to believe they are not clever, and they lose confidence. They stop trying, so they really do fall behind, and the belief comes true. The class also learns to treat them as less able, which is unfair to them.

keyPoints.label: Those left out lose confidence and believe they are less able
They stop trying, so they really do fall behind
The rest of the class starts treating them as less able too

subject: social-science
question: Name three grounds on which people in India have been treated unequally, and give an example of one of them.
modelAnswer: People have been treated unequally because of caste, with some barred from temples and wells. It has happened on grounds of religion, and on grounds of sex, when girls are kept from school. Disability and poverty are further grounds on which people are shut out.

keyPoints.label: Caste — barred from temples, wells or seating
Religion, or sex — girls kept from school
Disability, poverty or language are further grounds

subject: social-science
question: A village keeps two sets of drinking glasses at the tea stall, one for certain families. Explain what is wrong with this and what the law says.
modelAnswer: It is untouchability, which treats some people as impure because of the family they were born into. It insults their dignity and denies them equal treatment in a public place. The Constitution abolished untouchability, so the practice is a punishable offence.

keyPoints.label: It is untouchability, based on birth
It insults their dignity and denies equal treatment
The Constitution abolished it — it is a punishable offence

subject: social-science
question: "Boys do not cry." Explain what is wrong with saying this to a child, and what harm it does as they grow.
modelAnswer: Everyone feels sadness and pain, so it is simply untrue. It teaches a boy to hide what he feels instead of speaking about it, and hidden feelings build up. As a man he may find it hard to ask for help when he is struggling.

keyPoints.label: It is untrue — everyone feels sadness and pain
It teaches him to hide feelings instead of speaking
Later he may not ask for help when struggling

subject: social-science
question: A family sends its son for tuition but keeps its daughter at home to help with housework. Explain three ways this affects her whole life.
modelAnswer: She falls behind in her studies and may leave school altogether. Without qualifications she cannot take up work that pays well, so she stays dependent on others for money. Having no earnings of her own also leaves her with little say in decisions about her own life.

keyPoints.label: She falls behind and may leave school
Without qualifications she cannot get well-paid work
She stays dependent and has little say in her own life

subject: social-science
question: In some districts far fewer girls are born than boys. Explain what causes this and what trouble it stores up for society.
modelAnswer: Families that treat a daughter as a burden abort unborn girls, which is female foeticide. It is illegal, and finding out the sex of an unborn child before birth is banned. Over time it leaves far too few women, which unbalances society and makes life still harder for them.

keyPoints.label: Girls are seen as a burden, leading to female foeticide
It is illegal, and sex determination before birth is banned
It leaves too few women and unbalances society

subject: social-science
question: Give three things a country can do so that daughters are valued as much as sons.
modelAnswer: It can make schooling free and safe for girls so that every one of them studies. It can enforce laws against dowry and against testing the sex of an unborn child. It can also run campaigns that show women succeeding, so families see a daughter as a source of pride rather than a cost.

keyPoints.label: Make schooling free, safe and available to every girl
Enforce laws against dowry and sex determination
Campaigns showing women succeeding change attitudes

subject: social-science
question: Name two Indian women who reached the very top in their field, saying what each is known for and what their example proves.
modelAnswer: Kalpana Chawla became an astronaut and flew into space, the first woman of Indian origin to do so. Saina Nehwal reached the top of world badminton, and Indra Nooyi led one of the largest companies in the world. Their lives prove that ability has nothing to do with being a man or a woman.

keyPoints.label: Kalpana Chawla — astronaut, flew into space
Saina Nehwal, Indra Nooyi, Dipa Karmakar or similar
Ability has nothing to do with being a man or a woman

subject: social-science
question: Explain why it matters for a young person to see somebody like themselves succeeding at something difficult.
modelAnswer: It shows them the thing is actually possible, instead of something only other kinds of people do. It gives them the confidence to try, and someone to model themselves on. It also changes the minds of families and teachers, who then encourage them instead of holding them back.

keyPoints.label: It shows the thing is genuinely possible for them
It gives confidence and someone to model themselves on
It changes what families and teachers expect of them

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Describe what Dr B. R. Ambedkar faced as a schoolboy, and what he went on to achieve for the country.
modelAnswer: As a boy he was made to sit apart on a sack outside the classroom and was not allowed to drink from the common water pot. He studied abroad and became one of the most learned people of his time. He chaired the drafting committee of the Constitution and made sure it abolished untouchability and guaranteed equality.

keyPoints.label: Made to sit apart, refused water from the common pot
He studied abroad and became highly learned
He led the drafting of the Constitution and ended untouchability

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Dr Ambedkar said that political freedom alone was not enough for India. Explain what he meant.
modelAnswer: Freedom from British rule ended foreign control, but it did not end the unfair treatment of people at home. Millions were still kept out of temples, schools and wells because of the caste they were born into. He argued that real freedom needed social and economic equality as well, not just the right to vote.

keyPoints.label: Ending British rule removed foreign control only
Unfair treatment by caste continued inside the country
Real freedom needs social and economic equality too

subject: social-science
question: Explain what the Right to Equality guarantees an Indian citizen, and give two examples of what it forbids.
modelAnswer: It guarantees that everybody is equal before the law and gets its equal protection. The state may not treat a person differently because of religion, caste, sex, race or place of birth. It forbids untouchability and forbids barring anyone from shops, wells, roads or public places.

keyPoints.label: Everyone is equal before the law and equally protected by it
No different treatment by religion, caste, sex, race or birthplace
It forbids untouchability and barring people from public places

subject: social-science
question: If everyone is to be treated the same, explain why the government still reserves seats in colleges for certain communities.
modelAnswer: Some communities were held back for centuries and start from far behind everybody else. Treating unequal starting points identically would simply keep them behind for ever. Reservation is meant to help them catch up, so that equality becomes real and not just a promise on paper.

keyPoints.label: Some communities were held back for centuries
Treating unequal starting points identically keeps them behind
It helps them catch up so equality becomes real

subject: social-science
question: In April 2014 the Supreme Court gave an important judgement about a group long pushed to the margins. Describe what it decided and why it mattered.
modelAnswer: The Supreme Court recognised transgender people as a third gender in the NALSA judgement. It held that they have the same fundamental rights as anyone else, including the right to decide their own gender. It also directed that they be treated as socially and educationally backward so they get help in education and jobs.

keyPoints.label: Transgender people were recognised as a third gender
They hold the same fundamental rights, including self-identification
They were to get help in education and employment

subject: social-science
question: Describe three difficulties transgender people have faced in ordinary daily life in India.
modelAnswer: They have often been thrown out by their own families and left with nowhere to live. Schools and employers have refused them, so many were forced into begging to survive. They have also faced abuse in public and been denied proper treatment at hospitals.

keyPoints.label: Rejected by family and left without a home
Refused by schools and employers, pushed into begging
Abused in public and denied proper healthcare

subject: social-science
question: Describe how Jewish people were treated in Germany under Hitler, and what this shows about where prejudice can lead.
modelAnswer: They were stripped of citizenship and their rights, banned from many jobs and schools, and made to wear a yellow star so they could be picked out. They were forced into ghettos and then into concentration camps, where about six million were murdered in the Holocaust. It shows that prejudice left unchallenged can end in mass killing.

keyPoints.label: Citizenship, jobs and schooling were taken away; marked out by a star
Forced into ghettos and concentration camps
About six million died; prejudice unchallenged ends in killing

subject: social-science
question: Explain how ordinary Germans came to accept such cruelty, and what that teaches about staying silent.
modelAnswer: The government controlled newspapers, radio and schools, and repeated for years that one group was to blame for everything wrong. Children were taught it from a young age, so it seemed normal. Anyone who objected was punished, so most people stayed quiet — and silence let the cruelty grow.

keyPoints.label: Newspapers, radio and schools repeated the blame for years
Children were taught it young, so it seemed normal
Objectors were punished, so people stayed silent and it grew

subject: social-science
question: Explain what segregation meant in America, and describe one act of protest against it.
modelAnswer: Segregation kept black and white people apart by law, with separate schools, buses, parks and drinking fountains, and the ones for black people were far worse. Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger and was arrested. That began the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted over a year until the law was struck down.

keyPoints.label: People were kept apart by law — separate schools, buses, parks
What black people were given was far worse
Rosa Parks and the Montgomery bus boycott, or Martin Luther King

subject: social-science
question: A boycott simply means refusing to buy or use something. Explain why it can be such a powerful weapon for people with no other power.
modelAnswer: It costs the other side money, and losing income forces them to listen when nothing else would. It needs no weapons and no wealth, only that ordinary people agree to act together. It also draws the attention of newspapers and the wider public, so the unfairness becomes impossible to ignore.

keyPoints.label: It costs the other side money, which forces them to listen
It needs no weapons or wealth, only people acting together
It draws public and newspaper attention to the unfairness

subject: social-science
question: Imagine a town where nobody makes or enforces any rules. Describe what would go wrong, and what that tells you about why we have a government.
modelAnswer: Traffic would be chaos with nobody deciding which side to drive on, and disputes would be settled by whoever was strongest. Nobody would build roads, run hospitals or supply water, since no one person can afford to. A government exists to make rules, to settle quarrels fairly and to provide what no individual can provide alone.

keyPoints.label: Disorder — traffic chaos, the strongest getting their way
Nobody would build roads, hospitals or supply water
Government makes rules, settles disputes and provides for all

subject: social-science
question: Explain what it means to say a government has authority, and where that authority comes from in a democracy.
modelAnswer: Authority means its decisions bind everybody, and people can be punished for breaking them. In a democracy that power comes from the people themselves, who choose their representatives by voting. Because it is given by the people it can also be taken back at the next election.

keyPoints.label: Its decisions bind everyone, and breaking them is punished
In a democracy the power comes from the people, through voting
What the people give they can take back at an election

subject: social-science
question: Describe three quite different kinds of work a government does for its people, with an example of each.
modelAnswer: It keeps order and protects the country, through the police and the armed forces. It provides services nobody could provide alone, such as roads, schools, hospitals and water supply. It also settles disputes through the courts and looks after those in need, with pensions and relief after a flood.

keyPoints.label: Keeping order and defending the country — police and army
Providing roads, schools, hospitals and water
Settling disputes through courts, and helping those in need

subject: social-science
question: Where does a government get the money for all it does, and why must it account for how that money is spent?
modelAnswer: Most of it comes from taxes paid by citizens and businesses, along with fees and earnings from state undertakings. Because it is the public’s money, the public has a right to know where it went. Accounts are checked and placed before the legislature, which is how waste and corruption are caught.

keyPoints.label: Mainly taxes from citizens and businesses
It is the public’s money, so the public may ask where it went
Accounts are checked and placed before the legislature

subject: social-science
question: Explain why a country as large as India does not run everything from one office in the capital.
modelAnswer: The country is far too large and varied for one office to know what every place needs. A broken street light or a blocked drain is best handled by people living there. Splitting the work into levels also brings decisions closer to ordinary people, so they can be heard.

keyPoints.label: The country is too large and varied for one office
Local problems are best handled by people living there
It brings decisions closer to ordinary people

subject: social-science
question: A street light near your home has been out for weeks. Say who you would approach and why, rather than writing to the Prime Minister.
modelAnswer: The right body is the local one — the panchayat in a village or the municipality in a town. Street lighting is exactly the kind of small local matter it exists to handle, and its office is close by. The Prime Minister deals with the whole country and could not possibly attend to one lamp.

keyPoints.label: The panchayat or municipality — the local body
Street lighting is exactly its work, and its office is close by
The national level deals with the whole country

subject: social-science
question: Name the three levels at which India is governed and give one matter each one handles.
modelAnswer: At the top is the union level in Delhi, which handles defence, foreign affairs and currency. Then comes the state level, with its own assembly, handling police, farming and health. Below that is the local level — panchayats and municipalities — handling water supply, drains and street lighting.

keyPoints.label: Union or central level — defence, foreign affairs, currency
State level — police, agriculture, health
Local level — panchayats and municipalities, water, drains, lighting

subject: social-science
question: Explain what a panchayat is and describe two things it does for a village.
modelAnswer: A panchayat is the elected local body of a village, headed by a sarpanch and chosen by the villagers themselves. It looks after drinking water, roads, drains and street lighting. It also keeps records of births and deaths, runs schemes for work, and settles small local disputes.

keyPoints.label: An elected local body of the village, headed by a sarpanch
It looks after water, roads, drains and lighting
It keeps records, runs schemes and settles small disputes

subject: social-science
question: A government has three organs. Name them and say what each one does.
modelAnswer: The legislature makes the laws, and in India that is Parliament and the state assemblies. The executive carries them out, which is the Prime Minister, the ministers and the officials. The judiciary is the courts, which interpret the laws and settle disputes about them.

keyPoints.label: The legislature makes laws — Parliament and assemblies
The executive carries them out — ministers and officials
The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes — the courts

subject: social-science
question: Explain why the courts are kept separate from the ministers, and what would go wrong if they were not.
modelAnswer: Judges must be free to decide against the government itself when it breaks the law. If ministers controlled the judges, no one could ever win a case against those in power. Independence lets the courts protect citizens’ fundamental rights and check any misuse of authority.

keyPoints.label: Judges must be free to rule against the government itself
Otherwise nobody could win a case against those in power
Independence lets the courts protect fundamental rights

subject: social-science
question: Compare a democracy with a dictatorship in three ways.
modelAnswer: In a democracy the people choose their rulers by voting, while a dictator seizes power and is never chosen. A democracy allows criticism, free newspapers and opposition parties, whereas a dictatorship silences and jails those who object. In a democracy the rulers can be removed at the next election; a dictator cannot be removed peacefully.

keyPoints.label: People elect their rulers; a dictator seizes power
Criticism, free press and opposition are allowed, or crushed
Rulers can be voted out; a dictator cannot be removed peacefully

subject: social-science
question: In a monarchy, explain how the ruler comes to hold the position, and describe the difference between an absolute and a constitutional one.
modelAnswer: The ruler inherits the throne by birth, passing from parent to child rather than being chosen. In an absolute monarchy that ruler holds all the power and the word is law. In a constitutional monarchy the king or queen is only a ceremonial head, while an elected government actually governs, as in Britain.

keyPoints.label: The position is inherited by birth, not chosen
In an absolute one the ruler holds all the power
In a constitutional one the ruler is ceremonial, elected ministers govern

subject: social-science
topicLabel: The Quest for Universal Adult Franchise
question: Explain what universal adult franchise means, and name two groups who once had to fight for it.
modelAnswer: It means every adult citizen may vote, whatever their wealth, sex, caste, religion or education. Once only rich men who owned property were allowed to. Women had to fight for it, as did black people in South Africa and America, and poorer men without land.

keyPoints.label: Every adult citizen may vote, on equal terms
Regardless of wealth, sex, caste, religion or education
Women, black people, and men without property had to fight for it

subject: social-science
topicLabel: The Quest for Universal Adult Franchise
question: Explain why letting only property owners vote leads to unjust laws.
modelAnswer: Rulers listen to the people who can remove them, so they attend only to those who vote. Laws would then favour the wealthy — light taxes on land, little spending on the poor. Those with no vote have no way to be heard, so their needs are simply ignored.

keyPoints.label: Rulers attend only to those who can remove them
Laws would favour the wealthy over everyone else
Those without a vote have no way to be heard

subject: social-science
question: India gave every adult the vote from its very first election, which surprised the world. Explain why that was remarkable.
modelAnswer: Most of the population could not read or write, and other countries had assumed voting required education and wealth. Britain and America had taken over a century to widen the vote step by step, and women there had won it only recently. India granted it to everyone at once in 1950, treating the vote as a right rather than a reward.

keyPoints.label: Most people could not read or write, and were poor
Other countries had widened the vote slowly over a century
India granted it to all at once, as a right

subject: social-science
question: Describe two arrangements that let an Indian who cannot read still cast their vote properly.
modelAnswer: Every candidate is given a picture symbol, such as a hand or a lamp, which appears beside the name on the machine. Voters therefore recognise their choice without reading a word. Polling staff explain the machine, the ballot is secret, and an indelible ink mark prevents anyone voting twice.

keyPoints.label: Each candidate has a picture symbol on the machine
So voters recognise their choice without reading
Staff explain it, the ballot is secret, ink prevents voting twice

subject: social-science
question: Describe how women in Britain won the vote, and what they had to endure.
modelAnswer: Women campaigned for decades with petitions, meetings and marches, and were ignored. The suffragettes then took to breaking windows and chaining themselves to railings, and many were jailed and force-fed when they went on hunger strike. Their work, and the jobs women did during the First World War, finally won them the vote.

keyPoints.label: Decades of petitions, meetings and marches, all ignored
Then windows broken, chaining to railings — and jail
Their work and wartime jobs finally won them the vote

subject: social-science
question: What arguments were used against letting women vote, and why were they wrong?
modelAnswer: It was claimed that women were not intelligent enough to understand politics, which was simply false and rested on their being kept out of schools. It was said their place was the home and their husbands would decide for them, which denied them a mind of their own. Every country that gave women the vote showed the fears to be groundless.

keyPoints.label: The claim that they were not intelligent enough
The claim that their place was the home, husbands deciding
Both were false — kept from school, and later disproved everywhere

subject: social-science
question: Explain what apartheid was in South Africa and how it finally ended.
modelAnswer: Apartheid was a system of laws that separated people by race and gave power only to the white minority. Black South Africans were forced into poor areas, needed passes to travel and could not vote. After decades of protest, Nelson Mandela’s long imprisonment and pressure from other countries, it ended and he became president in 1994.

keyPoints.label: Laws separated people by race; power lay with the white minority
Black people were confined to poor areas, needed passes, could not vote
Protest, Mandela and outside pressure ended it; he became president

subject: social-science
question: Nelson Mandela spent twenty-seven years in prison, yet urged forgiveness on his release. Explain why that choice mattered so much.
modelAnswer: Revenge would have driven the country into a civil war between the races. By choosing reconciliation he persuaded people who had feared him that they had a place in the new nation. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission let the past be told openly, so the country could move on without tearing itself apart.

keyPoints.label: Revenge would have meant civil war between the races
Reconciliation gave former enemies a place in the new nation
A Truth and Reconciliation Commission let the past be told

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain what a globe is and give two reasons it shows our planet better than a flat map does.
modelAnswer: A globe is a small model of the earth, made round like the planet itself. Because it keeps that round form, the shapes and sizes of countries stay true, while a flat map stretches and distorts them. It also shows correct distances and directions, and how day and night follow each other.

keyPoints.label: It is a small round model of the earth
Shapes and sizes stay true; a flat map distorts them
Distances, directions, and day and night are shown properly

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The earth is not upright as it spins. Describe how it is held and what difference that makes.
modelAnswer: The earth is tilted about twenty-three and a half degrees from the upright, and it leans the same way all year. Because of that tilt, different parts lean towards the sun at different times of the year. That is what gives us the seasons — without it, every day everywhere would be alike.

keyPoints.label: It is tilted about 23½ degrees from the upright
It leans the same way throughout the year
The tilt is what gives us the seasons

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain what lines of latitude are and how they are numbered.
modelAnswer: They are imaginary circles drawn round the earth parallel to the equator, so they never meet. The equator is numbered zero, and the numbers rise to ninety degrees at each pole. Each one is marked north or south to say which side of the equator it lies on, and they get shorter towards the poles.

keyPoints.label: Imaginary circles parallel to the equator, never meeting
Zero at the equator, rising to 90 degrees at the poles
Each is labelled north or south of the equator

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Name the important parallels apart from the equator, and say what is special about the two at 23½ degrees.
modelAnswer: They are the Tropic of Cancer at 23½ north, the Tropic of Capricorn at 23½ south, and the Arctic and Antarctic Circles at 66½. The two tropics mark the furthest points at which the sun is ever directly overhead. Between them lies the hottest belt of the earth, which is why it is called the torrid zone.

keyPoints.label: Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn, Arctic and Antarctic Circles
The tropics mark the limits of an overhead sun
Between them is the hottest belt — the torrid zone

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain what meridians of longitude are, and how they differ from the lines that run round the earth sideways.
modelAnswer: Meridians are semicircles running from the north pole to the south pole, so they all meet at the poles. They are every one of them the same length, unlike parallels, which get shorter away from the equator. They are numbered from the prime meridian at zero out to a hundred and eighty degrees east and west.

keyPoints.label: Semicircles running pole to pole, meeting at the poles
All the same length, unlike parallels
Numbered from the prime meridian at 0 to 180 east and west

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The line numbered zero passes through Greenwich in London, and not through some other place. Explain why, and why the choice had to be agreed.
modelAnswer: There is no natural starting line for longitude, unlike latitude, which has the equator halfway between the poles. Countries once each used their own capital as zero, so the same place had different numbers on different maps and sailors could not compare them. In 1884 nations agreed on Greenwich, because Britain’s naval charts were already the most widely used.

keyPoints.label: There is no natural zero for longitude, unlike the equator for latitude
Countries each used their own, so maps disagreed
Nations agreed on Greenwich in 1884

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A ship radios that it is sinking and gives two numbers. Explain how those two numbers let rescuers find it anywhere on the planet.
modelAnswer: The two numbers are its latitude and its longitude. Latitude fixes how far north or south of the equator it is, and longitude fixes how far east or west of the prime meridian. Only one point on earth has that pair of values, where the two lines cross, so the position is exact.

keyPoints.label: They are latitude and longitude
One fixes north–south, the other east–west
Only one point has that pair — where the two lines cross

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why giving only one of the two numbers is useless for finding a place.
modelAnswer: One value on its own describes a whole line, not a point. Every place along that circle shares the same reading, and thousands of towns could lie on it. Only when the second value is added do the two lines cross at a single spot.

keyPoints.label: One value describes a whole line, not a point
Every place along it shares that reading
Only both together cross at a single spot

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The earth makes two quite different movements. Name them and say what each one produces.
modelAnswer: Rotation is the earth spinning on its own axis, once in about twenty-four hours, and it gives us day and night. Revolution is the earth travelling round the sun, once in about three hundred and sixty-five days, and it gives us the year and the seasons. The extra quarter day each year is why we add a leap day.

keyPoints.label: Rotation — spinning on its axis in 24 hours
Rotation gives day and night
Revolution — round the sun in 365¼ days, giving the year and seasons

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why we add an extra day to February every fourth year.
modelAnswer: The earth actually takes about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days to go once round the sun. A calendar year is kept at three hundred and sixty-five whole days, so a quarter of a day is left over each time. Four of those quarters make one whole day, which is added as the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year.

keyPoints.label: One trip round the sun takes 365¼ days
The calendar uses 365 whole days, leaving a quarter over
Four quarters make a whole day — 29 February in a leap year

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: When India is having summer, Australia is having winter. Explain how that can be.
modelAnswer: The earth is tilted, so at any time one half leans towards the sun and the other leans away. The half leaning towards it gets more direct rays and longer days, and has summer. Half a year later the earth is on the other side of its orbit and the position is reversed, so the two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.

keyPoints.label: The earth is tilted, so one half leans towards the sun
The half leaning towards it gets direct rays and longer days
The other half leans away, so the hemispheres are opposite

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Name what happens on 21 March and 23 September, and say how those dates differ from 21 June and 22 December.
modelAnswer: On the twenty-first of March and the twenty-third of September the sun is directly over the equator, and these are the equinoxes, when day and night are equal everywhere. On the twenty-first of June the sun is over the Tropic of Cancer, and on the twenty-second of December over the Tropic of Capricorn, and these are the solstices. At a solstice the difference between day and night is at its greatest.

keyPoints.label: The equinoxes — sun over the equator, day and night equal
The solstices — sun over a tropic
At a solstice the day–night difference is greatest

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The earth is divided into three heat belts. Name them and explain what makes each one hot or cold.
modelAnswer: The torrid zone lies between the two tropics, where the sun is overhead at some time of the year, so it is the hottest. The temperate zones lie between the tropics and the polar circles, where the rays are slanting and the climate is moderate. The frigid zones lie beyond the polar circles, where the rays are very slanting and it is bitterly cold.

keyPoints.label: Torrid — between the tropics, sun overhead, hottest
Temperate — moderate, with slanting rays
Frigid — beyond the polar circles, very slanting rays, bitterly cold

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why the poles stay so cold even during their long summer when the sun never sets.
modelAnswer: The sun there is always low down near the horizon, so its rays strike at a very slanting angle. Slanting rays spread the same amount of heat over a much larger area, so each patch of ground gets little. The ice and snow also reflect most of the light straight back, and the rays pass through more of the atmosphere on the way in.

keyPoints.label: The sun stays low, so the rays strike very slantingly
Slanting rays spread the heat over a larger area
Ice and snow reflect most of it, and it crosses more atmosphere

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
topicLabel: Varying Lengths of Day and Night
question: In Delhi a June day is much longer than a December one, but at the equator every day is the same. Explain both facts.
modelAnswer: The earth’s tilt means that in June the northern half leans towards the sun, so more of its circle of latitude lies in daylight and the day is long. In December it leans away, so the day is short. The equator is cut exactly in half by the circle of illumination whatever the tilt, so it always has about twelve hours of each.

keyPoints.label: In June the northern half leans towards the sun, so days are long
More of the latitude circle lies in daylight
The equator is always cut in half, so it gets about twelve hours each

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
topicLabel: Varying Lengths of Day and Night
question: In parts of Norway the sun does not set for weeks in summer. Explain how that happens and what occurs there in winter.
modelAnswer: Those places lie beyond the Arctic Circle, and in summer that whole region leans towards the sun. It stays inside the lit half of the earth right through a full rotation, so the sun never dips below the horizon and it is called the land of the midnight sun. In winter the tilt is the other way and the region stays in darkness, with no sunrise for weeks.

keyPoints.label: The place lies beyond the Arctic Circle, leaning towards the sun
It stays in the lit half through a whole rotation
In winter it stays in darkness, with no sunrise for weeks

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why India keeps a single clock time from Gujarat to Assam, even though the sun rises in one nearly two hours before the other.
modelAnswer: Every meridian has its own local time set by the sun, so strictly each town would differ. Running railways, offices and broadcasts with thousands of different clock readings would be impossible. So one meridian is picked for the whole country — 82½ degrees east, through Mirzapur — and its local time becomes standard time everywhere.

keyPoints.label: Each meridian has its own local time set by the sun
Thousands of different clock readings would make life impossible
One meridian — 82½° E — is adopted for the whole country

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain what GMT means and why the world needed one agreed reference clock.
modelAnswer: It is the time on the prime meridian at Greenwich, from which every country’s time is measured as so many hours ahead or behind. Without one agreed reference there would be no way to state when an international flight lands or a broadcast begins. India, for instance, is five and a half hours ahead of it.

keyPoints.label: The time on the prime meridian at Greenwich
Every country is so many hours ahead of or behind it
Without a common reference, flights and broadcasts could not be timed

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Without doing any sum, explain the method for working out how far ahead one place is of another when you know both their meridians.
modelAnswer: The earth turns once, three hundred and sixty degrees, in twenty-four hours, so it covers fifteen degrees in an hour and one degree in four minutes. Find the difference between the two readings, remembering to add them if the places are on opposite sides of the prime meridian. Multiply that difference by four minutes, and the place lying further east is ahead.

keyPoints.label: 360° in 24 hours means 15° an hour, or 1° in four minutes
Take the difference between the two readings, adding if opposite sides
Multiply out, and the place further east is ahead

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why places lying to the east see the sun earlier, using the way the planet turns.
modelAnswer: The earth spins from west to east, so a place on the eastern side is carried into the sunlight first. Sunrise therefore reaches the east before the west, and its clock is ahead. That is why the sun rises in Assam well before it rises in Gujarat.

keyPoints.label: The earth spins from west to east
So eastern places are carried into the sunlight first
Their clocks are therefore ahead

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A cousin in London wants to telephone you in India. Explain the reasoning you would use to tell them a good hour to ring, without giving a number.
modelAnswer: India runs five and a half hours ahead of the time in London. So whatever their clock says, ours says five and a half hours more, and their morning is already our afternoon. They must therefore ring earlier in their day than feels natural, or they will be telephoning in the middle of our night.

keyPoints.label: India is five and a half hours ahead
Add that gap to their clock to get ours
So they must ring earlier in their day, or it is our night

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A traveller flies from Delhi to New York and arrives at a clock time earlier than when they took off. Explain how that is possible.
modelAnswer: New York lies far to the west of Delhi, so its clocks run many hours behind. The flight takes many hours, but crossing westwards the traveller is putting the clock back further than the hours actually spent flying. No time is really gained — only the reading on the clock has changed, because they moved into a different zone.

keyPoints.label: New York is far west, so its clocks are hours behind
Travelling west means putting the clock back more than the flight took
No time is really gained — only the clock reading changed

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain what the International Date Line is, where it runs, and what a traveller must do on crossing it.
modelAnswer: It is an imaginary line roughly along the meridian of a hundred and eighty degrees, out in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Crossing it going west, a traveller adds a day, and crossing it going east, they take one off. It bends around islands and countries so that no inhabited place is split between two dates.

keyPoints.label: Roughly along 180°, in the middle of the Pacific
Going west a day is added; going east a day is dropped
It bends around land so no country is split between two dates

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Explain why the world needs such a line at all, using what happens as you keep travelling in one direction.
modelAnswer: Going west, the clock is put back an hour for every fifteen degrees, and after going right round the whole twenty-four hours have been taken off. The traveller would arrive back having lost a whole day compared with the people who stayed at home. A place is therefore fixed where the date is changed, so the calendar comes out right.

keyPoints.label: An hour is gained or lost every 15 degrees
Right round the world that adds up to a whole 24 hours
So one place is fixed where the date changes, keeping calendars right

subject: social-science
question: Describe how the Harappan civilisation came to be found again after thousands of years.
modelAnswer: Workers building a railway line in Punjab in the eighteen fifties carried away old baked bricks from a mound to use as ballast, not knowing what they were. In the nineteen twenties archaeologists including Daya Ram Sahni and R. D. Banerji excavated Harappa and Mohenjodaro. Sir John Marshall announced that a civilisation as old as Egypt and Mesopotamia had been found in India.

keyPoints.label: Railway builders carried away ancient bricks from a mound
Archaeologists excavated Harappa and Mohenjodaro in the 1920s
It proved a civilisation as old as Egypt or Mesopotamia

subject: social-science
question: Give three explanations historians offer for why those great cities were abandoned.
modelAnswer: Rivers may have changed course or dried up, so the water supply failed. Forests were cut down for firewood and to bake bricks, and heavy grazing wore out the land, so harvests fell. Floods, earthquakes and a breakdown of trade have all been suggested as well, and no single cause is agreed.

keyPoints.label: Rivers changed course or dried up
Deforestation and grazing wore out the land, so harvests fell
Floods, earthquakes or a collapse of trade are also suggested

subject: social-science
question: Describe how a Harappan city was laid out, and what that tells us about the people who built it.
modelAnswer: The city was built in two parts, a raised citadel on the west and a larger lower town on the east where most people lived. Streets ran straight and crossed one another at right angles, dividing the town into neat blocks. Such careful planning shows there was a strong authority able to decide and enforce how the whole city was built.

keyPoints.label: A raised citadel and a larger lower town
Straight streets crossing at right angles, in neat blocks
Such planning implies a strong central authority

subject: social-science
question: The drainage of these cities is often called their greatest achievement. Describe it and say why it impresses people so much.
modelAnswer: Every house had its own bathing area and drain, connected to covered channels running under the streets. The channels were laid with a gentle slope so the water flowed away, and manholes were left at intervals so they could be cleaned. It impresses because it served ordinary homes and not just palaces, and many towns today still lack anything as good.

keyPoints.label: Each house drained into covered channels under the streets
Laid on a slope, with manholes for cleaning
It served ordinary homes, and many towns today lack as much

subject: social-science
question: Describe how the Harappan people made their living, mentioning three kinds of work.
modelAnswer: Many were farmers, growing wheat, barley, peas and cotton, and keeping cattle, sheep and buffalo. Craftspeople made pottery, beads of carnelian, copper and bronze tools, and wove cotton cloth. Traders carried goods to Mesopotamia and brought back metals, and weights and seals show the trade was carefully regulated.

keyPoints.label: Farming — wheat, barley, peas, cotton — and keeping animals
Crafts — pottery, beads, copper and bronze tools, weaving
Trade with Mesopotamia, regulated by weights and seals

subject: social-science
question: Archaeologists say Harappan society was well organised without evidence of kings or armies. Explain what makes them think so.
modelAnswer: Weights and measures were standard across cities hundreds of miles apart, which means somebody was enforcing a common system. Bricks everywhere were made to the same proportions, and the town planning was uniform. Yet almost no weapons, no grand palaces and no royal tombs have been found, so the authority does not look like a warrior king.

keyPoints.label: Standard weights and measures across distant cities
Bricks and town planning followed the same pattern everywhere
Almost no weapons, palaces or royal tombs have been found

subject: social-science
question: Describe what a Harappan seal was made of and what it was used for.
