modelAnswer: Most were cut from steatite, a soft stone, and were small enough to hold in the palm. Each carried an animal figure and a short line of signs above it. Pressed into wet clay on a bundle of goods, the seal left a mark showing who had sent it and that the bundle had not been opened.

keyPoints.label: Cut from steatite, a soft stone, and small enough to hold
An animal figure and a short line of signs
Pressed into wet clay to mark ownership and show goods were unopened

subject: social-science
question: Thousands of pieces of Harappan writing survive, yet nobody can read a word of it. Explain why.
modelAnswer: The inscriptions are extremely short, most only a few signs long, so there is little to work from. There is no bilingual text pairing it with a language we already know, as the Rosetta Stone gave for Egyptian. Nobody knows what language it recorded either, and the signs are too many to be an alphabet.

keyPoints.label: The inscriptions are very short, only a few signs each
There is no bilingual text, as the Rosetta Stone gave for Egypt
The language behind it is unknown, and the signs are too many for an alphabet

subject: social-science
question: The animal most often carved on these seals is a one-horned creature scholars call the unicorn. Say what else appears beside it and why the carvings matter to us.
modelAnswer: Beside the animal there is usually a short row of signs, and often an object in front of it that may be a feeding trough or a stand for offerings. The carvings matter because they are among the finest art these people left, and they tell us which animals mattered to them. They also carry almost all the surviving samples of their writing.

keyPoints.label: A short row of signs, and an object like a trough before the animal
They are fine art and show which animals mattered
They carry nearly all the surviving writing

subject: social-science
question: A seal shows a figure seated cross-legged surrounded by animals. Explain what scholars have suggested about it, and why they cannot be certain.
modelAnswer: Some have suggested the seated figure is a god, sometimes called a proto-Shiva, because the pose resembles later images of Shiva as lord of the beasts. Others say it may be a chief, a priest or simply a scene from a story. Nobody can be sure, because the writing cannot be read and there is nothing to confirm any of the guesses.

keyPoints.label: It may be a god — sometimes called proto-Shiva, lord of beasts
It might instead be a chief, a priest or a scene from a story
Certainty is impossible while the script cannot be read

subject: english
question:
Read these lines and explain what the poet is showing you, and how:

“A little lane, the brook runs close beside
And spangles in the sunshine while the fish glide swiftly by
And hedges leafing with the green spring tide”
modelAnswer: The poet is showing a small stream running along the edge of the lane, throwing back points of sunlight as it moves. The fish are gliding smoothly through it, which makes the water feel alive rather than still. Meanwhile the hedges are putting out new leaves, so the whole scene is one of a place quietly coming to life in spring.

keyPoints.label: The stream throws back points of sunlight as it moves
The fish move smoothly, so the water feels alive
New leaves on the hedges — the place is coming to life

subject: english
question:
Read these lines and explain what they tell you about the season, and why:

“How mild the Spring comes in; the daisy buds
Lift up their golden blossoms to the sky
How lovely are the pingles and the woods”
modelAnswer: The season is arriving gently, with no harshness of cold or storm, which is what mild means here. The daisy buds are opening and raising their yellow flowers upward, as though reaching deliberately, so the poet gives the flowers a human action. Looking about at the small fields and the woods, he finds the whole scene beautiful.

keyPoints.label: The season arrives gently — no harshness or storm
The buds open and raise their yellow flowers upward
Giving flowers a human action is personification

subject: english
question:
Read these closing lines and explain what the poet is claiming, and how he earns it:

“Here a beetle runs; and there a fly
Rests on the Arum leaf in bottle green
And all the Spring in this Sweet lane is seen”
modelAnswer: He is claiming that the whole of the season can be found in this one small lane. He earns it by noticing the very smallest things — a beetle running, a single fly on a dark green leaf — rather than anything grand. Looking that closely at one ordinary place is what shows it holds everything.

keyPoints.label: The whole season is contained in one small lane
He notices the very smallest creatures and details
An ordinary place, looked at closely, is enough

subject: english
question: The whole poem stays inside one lane. Explain how the poet still makes it feel like the whole of springtime.
modelAnswer: He fills it with many different living things — fish, birds, flowers, a beetle, a fly — so there is life at every level from the water to the sky. He shows things beginning rather than finished, like the robin with its nest only started and the buds just opening. And he uses colour throughout, the golden blossoms and the pale blue sky and the bottle green leaf, so the reader sees it all at once.

keyPoints.label: Many different living things, from the water to the sky
Things are beginning rather than finished — nest, buds
Colour throughout — golden, pale blue, bottle green
